title: Mamon tostado
intro: Small sponge cakes baked once until golden, then again at low heat until dry and crunchy all the way through. Light, crisp and buttery, like a sweet toasted sponge cookie.

items.name: butter
items.note: melted, plus more for the molds

steps.text: Heat the oven to 180°C (350°F). Brush 24 small oval or rectangular molds, or two mini muffin tins, with butter.

Beat the eggs and sugar with an electric mixer on high until very thick, pale and tripled in volume, and the batter falls in a ribbon that holds for a few seconds, about 8 minutes. Beat in the vanilla.
Sift the flour and salt over the eggs in two additions, folding gently each time. Fold a spoonful of batter into the melted butter, then fold that back into the batter.
Fill the molds about two thirds full and bake until golden and springy.
Unmold onto a rack and lower the oven to 150°C (300°F). Cool the cakes for 10 minutes.
Brush the tops lightly with melted butter, arrange on a tray and bake again, turning once, until dry, crisp and deep golden throughout.
Cool completely on the tray, then store in an airtight jar.

tips: Break one open to check: it should be crunchy to the center. If not, give the batch 5 to 10 minutes more at low heat.

title: Taisan
intro: A tall, airy chiffon loaf baked in a loaf pan and finished with butter and sugar, sometimes with grated cheese. Soft and lightly sweet, it is sliced thick for merienda.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 160°C (325°F). Line a 23 x 13 cm (9 x 5 inch) loaf pan with parchment, leaving some overhang.
Sift the flour, baking powder and salt. Whisk the yolks with 60 g sugar until pale, then whisk in the oil, milk and vanilla. Whisk in the flour until smooth.
Beat the egg whites with the cream of tartar until foamy, then add 80 g sugar gradually and beat to stiff, glossy peaks.
Fold the meringue into the batter in three additions, gently, until no white streaks remain. Pour into the pan and smooth the top.
Bake until tall, golden and a skewer in the center comes out clean.
Cool in the pan for 10 minutes, then lift out by the parchment. While still warm, spread the top with butter and sprinkle with sugar and cheese.
Cool completely before slicing with a serrated knife.

tips: A crack along the top is normal. Keep taisan wrapped at room temperature and eat within 3 days.

title: Broas
intro: Light, crisp ladyfinger-style sponge biscuits with a crackly sugar top. They are dry and airy, good with coffee or hot chocolate, and are also used to layer icebox cakes.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 180°C (350°F). Line two baking trays with parchment and fit a piping bag with a 1 cm (1/2 inch) round tip.
Beat the egg whites with the salt until foamy, then add 50 g sugar gradually and beat to stiff, glossy peaks.
In another bowl, beat the yolks with the remaining 50 g sugar and the vanilla until thick and pale.
Fold the yolks into the whites, then sift the flour over and fold gently until just combined.
Pipe fingers about 8 cm (3 inches) long, 3 cm (1 inch) apart. Dust generously with powdered sugar.
Bake until golden and firm to the touch.
Cool on the trays; they firm up and crisp as they cool. Store airtight.

tips: For extra-crisp broas, turn off the oven after baking and leave them inside with the door ajar for 20 minutes.

title: Lengua de gato
intro: Thin, crisp butter cookies piped into long tongue shapes and baked until the edges turn golden. Delicate, buttery and a little crunchy, they are a common gift tin cookie.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 180°C (350°F). Line two baking trays with parchment.
Beat the butter and powdered sugar until pale and fluffy, about 3 minutes.
Beat in the egg whites one at a time, then the vanilla. The mixture may look curdled; it comes together once the flour goes in.
Fold in the flour and salt until smooth.
Spoon into a piping bag with a small round tip and pipe thin strips about 6 cm (2 1/2 inches) long, 4 cm (1 1/2 inches) apart, as they spread.
Bake one tray at a time until the edges are golden brown and the centers pale.
Cool on the tray for 1 minute, then move to a rack. Store airtight once cold.

tips: Pipe them thin and evenly; thicker cookies stay soft in the middle. If they soften in humid weather, crisp them in a 150°C (300°F) oven for 5 minutes.

title: Uraro
intro: Pale arrowroot cookies that crumble and melt on the tongue, with a gentle butter and coconut flavor. They are pressed or piped into little flowers and baked without browning.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 160°C (325°F). Line two baking trays with parchment.
Beat the butter and powdered sugar until creamy. Beat in the yolks, coconut milk and vanilla.
Add the arrowroot flour and salt and mix into a soft, smooth dough. If it is too stiff to pipe, add a teaspoon of coconut milk at a time.
Pipe small rosettes with a star tip, or press through a cookie press, about 3 cm (1 inch) apart.
Bake one tray at a time until set and dry on the bottom but still pale on top.
Cool completely on the tray; they are fragile while warm. Store airtight.

tips: Use pure arrowroot flour, not cornstarch, for the right melt-in-the-mouth texture. Do not let them brown; they turn hard and lose their delicate flavor.

title: Rosquillos
intro: Crisp, lightly sweet cookies cut into scalloped rings with a hole in the middle. They are crunchy and plain in a good way, made for dunking in coffee or hot chocolate.

steps.text: Whisk the flour, baking powder and salt together.
Beat the butter and sugar until creamy. Beat in the eggs one at a time, then the vanilla.
Mix in the flour, adding just enough milk to form a firm, smooth dough. Wrap and chill until firm.
Heat the oven to 180°C (350°F) and line two trays. Roll the dough on a floured counter to about 5 mm (1/4 inch) thick.
Cut out cookies with a 5 cm (2 inch) scalloped round cutter, then punch a small hole in the center of each with a piping tip or a straw. Reroll the scraps once.
Bake one tray at a time until light golden at the edges.
Cool completely on a rack; they crisp as they cool. Store in an airtight jar.

tips: Roll the dough evenly so all the cookies bake at the same rate. They keep for 2 weeks in a sealed jar.

title: Barquillos
intro: Paper-thin wafers rolled into tubes while still hot, so they set crisp and hollow. Sweet, buttery and fragile, they are eaten on their own or tucked into ice cream.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 180°C (350°F). Line a baking tray with a silicone mat or parchment. Have a wooden spoon handle or a 1 cm (1/2 inch) dowel ready.
Whisk the egg whites and sugar until the sugar dissolves and the mix is frothy. Whisk in the butter, milk and vanilla, then the flour, until smooth.
Rest the batter so it thickens slightly.
Drop 4 level tablespoons of batter on the tray, well apart, and spread each into a very thin 10 cm (4 inch) circle with the back of the spoon.
Bake until the edges are golden and the centers just colored.

Working fast, lift one wafer with a thin spatula and roll it tightly around the spoon handle. Slide it off and let it cool on a rack. Repeat with the rest. If they harden before you roll them, return the tray to the oven for 30 seconds.
Repeat with the remaining batter, baking 4 at a time. Store in an airtight jar once cold.

tips: Bake only a few at a time; you have about 20 seconds to roll each one. A pizzelle iron also works: cook a spoonful for about 1 minute and roll at once.

title: Chocolate crinkles
intro: Soft, fudgy chocolate cookies rolled in powdered sugar so they bake up with white cracks across a dark top. Chewy inside, lightly crisp outside, and very chocolatey.

steps.text: Whisk the flour, cocoa, baking powder and salt together.
In a large bowl, whisk the sugar and oil, then whisk in the eggs one at a time and the vanilla.
Stir in the dry ingredients until no streaks remain. The dough will be very soft. Cover and chill until firm.
Heat the oven to 175°C (350°F) and line two trays with parchment.
Scoop the dough into 24 balls of about 1 tablespoon. Roll each in powdered sugar until thickly coated, and set 5 cm (2 inches) apart.
Bake one tray at a time until puffed and cracked, with edges set but centers still soft.
Cool on the tray for 5 minutes, then move to a rack.

tips: Chilling is what keeps the cracks white; warm dough melts the sugar. The dough keeps for 3 days in the fridge, so you can bake in batches.

title: Food for the gods
intro: Chewy, buttery bars packed with chopped dates and walnuts, a favorite to give away in little wrapped squares at Christmas. Rich with brown sugar and caramel flavor.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 175°C (350°F). Line a 20 cm (8 inch) square pan with parchment.
Whisk the flour, baking powder and salt together. Toss the dates and walnuts with a tablespoon of the flour mixture so they do not sink.
Whisk the melted butter and brown sugar until smooth. Whisk in the eggs and vanilla.
Stir in the flour mixture, then fold in the dates and walnuts. Spread evenly in the pan.
Bake until golden and a toothpick in the center comes out with a few moist crumbs.
Cool completely in the pan before cutting into 16 squares.

tips: Chill the cooled slab for 30 minutes for clean cuts. Wrap squares individually in cellophane; they keep for a week at room temperature.

title: Revel bars
intro: Chewy oatmeal cookie bars with a thick layer of fudgy chocolate and condensed milk baked in the middle. Sweet, rich and easy to make in one big pan.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 175°C (350°F). Grease and line a 23 x 33 cm (9 x 13 inch) pan.
Beat the butter and brown sugar until creamy. Beat in the eggs and vanilla.
Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt, then stir them in with the oats until evenly mixed.
Melt the chocolate chips, condensed milk, butter and salt in a pan over low heat, stirring, until smooth.
Press two thirds of the oat dough into the pan. Spread the chocolate over it to within 1 cm (1/2 inch) of the edges, then drop the rest of the oat dough in small pieces over the top.
Bake until the top is golden; the chocolate will still look soft.
Cool completely in the pan before cutting into 24 bars.

tips: For neat bars, chill the cooled pan for an hour before cutting. Keep them in a sealed container for up to 5 days.

title: Buko pie
intro: A double-crust pie filled with tender strips of young coconut in a creamy, milky filling. The flaky crust and soft, sweet coconut make it a favorite pasalubong.

steps.text: Make the crust: mix the flour, sugar and salt, then rub in the butter until it looks like coarse crumbs with some pea-size bits. Add ice water a tablespoon at a time until the dough just holds together.
Divide into two discs, one slightly bigger, wrap and chill.

Make the filling: whisk the coconut water, condensed milk, evaporated milk, cornstarch and sugar in a pan until smooth. Add the coconut and cook over medium heat, stirring, until thick and glossy, about 5 minutes. Cool.
Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Roll the bigger disc out and line a 23 cm (9 inch) pie plate, leaving a little overhang.
Spoon in the cooled filling. Roll out the second disc, lay it over the top, trim, and crimp the edges to seal. Cut a few slits in the top and brush with beaten egg.
Bake for 15 minutes, then lower the heat to 180°C (350°F).
Bake until the crust is deep golden.
Cool for at least 1 hour before slicing so the filling sets.

tips: Use soft, young coconut that bends rather than snaps. Store the pie in the fridge and warm slices briefly in the oven to crisp the crust.

title: Egg pie
intro: A bakery-style pie with a buttery crust and a smooth, sweet egg custard that bakes up with a browned top. Creamy and comforting, it is served cool in wedges.

steps.text: Mix the flour, sugar and salt, rub in the butter until crumbly, and add ice water until the dough holds together. Flatten into a disc, wrap and chill.
Roll the dough out and line a 23 cm (9 inch) pie plate. Crimp the edge and prick the base with a fork. Chill while you make the filling.
Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Whisk 2 whole eggs and 2 yolks with the sugar until the sugar dissolves. Whisk in the evaporated milk, fresh milk and vanilla, then strain into a jug.
Beat the 2 reserved egg whites to soft peaks and gently fold them into the custard. They rise to the top and form the browned crust.
Pour the filling into the crust and bake for 10 minutes.
Lower the heat to 160°C (325°F) and bake until the top is golden brown and the center jiggles only slightly when nudged.
Cool to room temperature, then chill before slicing.

tips: Do not overbake: the custard sets further as it cools, and too much heat makes it watery and pitted. Keep egg pie in the fridge for up to 3 days.

title: Silvanas
intro: Frozen sandwiches of crisp cashew meringue wafers and silky buttercream, coated in fine cookie crumbs. Crunchy, chewy, buttery and best eaten cold from the freezer.

items.name: fine cookie crumbs
items.note: from plain biscuits such as Marie, mixed with any broken wafers

steps.text: Heat the oven to 150°C (300°F) and line two trays with parchment. Mix the ground cashews with the flour.
Beat the egg whites with the cream of tartar until foamy, add the sugar gradually and beat to stiff, glossy peaks. Fold in the cashew mixture gently.
Pipe or spread 32 ovals about 7 x 4 cm (3 x 1 1/2 inches) and 5 mm (1/4 inch) thick on the trays.
Bake until dry, crisp and lightly golden, and the wafers lift off the paper cleanly. Cool completely.
For the buttercream, boil the sugar and water until the syrup reaches 115°C (240°F), the soft-ball stage. Meanwhile, beat the yolks until pale.

With the mixer running, pour the hot syrup in a thin stream into the yolks. Keep beating until the bowl feels cool, about 8 minutes. Beat in the butter a tablespoon at a time, then the vanilla, until smooth and fluffy.
Sandwich pairs of wafers with a thick layer of buttercream. Spread a thin layer over the outside of each sandwich and roll it in the crumbs.
Freeze on a tray until firm, then wrap individually.

tips: Silvanas keep for a month in the freezer. Serve straight from the freezer or after 5 minutes at room temperature.

title: Sans rival
intro: Layers of crisp, chewy cashew meringue stacked with rich French buttercream and covered in chopped toasted cashews. It is very sweet and buttery, and served cold in small slices.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 150°C (300°F). Draw three 20 x 30 cm (8 x 12 inch) rectangles on parchment, turn the paper over and set it on baking trays. Grease lightly.
Beat the egg whites with the cream of tartar until foamy, add the sugar gradually and beat to stiff, glossy peaks. Fold in the finely chopped cashews.
Spread the meringue evenly inside the three rectangles.
Bake until golden, dry and crisp, swapping the trays halfway. Cool on the paper, then peel it off carefully.
For the buttercream, boil the sugar and water to 115°C (240°F), the soft-ball stage. Beat the yolks until pale, then pour in the hot syrup in a thin stream with the mixer running. Beat until cool.
Beat in the butter a tablespoon at a time, then the vanilla, until thick and smooth.
Trim the meringue sheets to the same size. Stack them with buttercream between each layer, then cover the top and sides with the rest.
Press the coarsely chopped cashews over the top and sides. Chill until firm.
Slice with a sharp knife dipped in hot water and serve cold.

tips: If the buttercream looks curdled, keep beating; it comes together. Sans rival keeps for a week in the fridge and freezes well.

title: Ube chiffon cake
intro: A tall, feather-light purple chiffon cake flavored with ube halaya and coconut milk. Moist, gently sweet and fragrant, it is good plain or with a light frosting.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 160°C (325°F). Have an ungreased 25 cm (10 inch) tube pan ready; the batter needs bare sides to climb.
Sift the cake flour, baking powder and salt.
Whisk the yolks with 100 g sugar until pale. Whisk in the oil, coconut milk, ube halaya and ube flavoring until smooth, then whisk in the flour mixture.
Beat the egg whites with the cream of tartar until foamy, add 100 g sugar gradually and beat to stiff, glossy peaks.
Fold a third of the meringue into the ube batter, then fold in the rest gently until evenly purple with no white streaks.
Pour into the pan, run a skewer through the batter to pop large bubbles, and smooth the top.
Bake until risen, springy and a skewer comes out clean.
Turn the pan upside down at once and cool completely, about 1 1/2 hours. Run a thin knife around the sides and center to release.

tips: Cooling upside down keeps the cake from sinking. Wrapped well, it stays moist for 3 days at room temperature.

title: Pandan chiffon cake
intro: A pale green chiffon cake made with fresh pandan juice and coconut milk, light and springy with a sweet, grassy vanilla-like fragrance.

steps.text: Blend the pandan leaves with the water until finely chopped, then squeeze through a cloth or fine sieve. Measure 80 ml of juice, topping up with water if needed.
Heat the oven to 160°C (325°F). Have an ungreased 25 cm (10 inch) tube pan ready.
Sift the cake flour, baking powder and salt.
Whisk the yolks with 100 g sugar until pale. Whisk in the oil, coconut milk, pandan juice and extract, then the flour mixture, until smooth.
Beat the egg whites with the cream of tartar until foamy, add 100 g sugar gradually and beat to stiff, glossy peaks.
Fold the meringue into the batter in three additions, gently, until evenly green. Pour into the pan and smooth the top.
Bake until risen, golden on top and a skewer comes out clean.
Invert the pan at once and cool completely before releasing the cake with a thin knife.

tips: Frozen pandan leaves from Asian groceries work as well as fresh. The cake is good plain or with lightly sweetened whipped cream.

title: Mocha cake
intro: Soft coffee chiffon layers filled and covered with a whipped mocha buttercream, in the style of Filipino bakeshop celebration cakes. Light, not too sweet and full of coffee flavor.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 160°C (325°F). Line the bottoms of two 20 cm (8 inch) round pans with parchment; do not grease the sides. Dissolve 2 tablespoons instant coffee in the hot water and cool.
Sift the flour, baking powder and salt. Whisk the yolks with 80 g sugar until pale, then whisk in the oil, coffee and the flour mixture until smooth.
Beat the egg whites with the cream of tartar until foamy, add 100 g sugar gradually and beat to stiff, glossy peaks. Fold into the coffee batter in three additions.
Divide between the pans and bake until springy and a skewer comes out clean.
Invert the pans onto a rack and cool completely, then run a knife around the sides and release.
For the buttercream, beat the butter until pale, about 3 minutes. Beat in the powdered sugar and cocoa, then the cooled coffee and evaporated milk, until light and fluffy.
Set one layer on a plate, spread with a thick layer of buttercream, and top with the second layer. Cover the top and sides with the rest, piping a border if you like.
Chill to set the frosting, then let it stand 15 minutes before slicing.

tips: Brush each layer with a little sweetened brewed coffee before frosting for a moister cake. Store covered in the fridge for up to 4 days.

title: Ube roll
intro: A soft purple chiffon sponge rolled around a thick layer of creamy ube halaya. Sweet, moist and pretty in slices, it is a favorite for parties and gifts.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 170°C (340°F). Line a 25 x 38 cm (10 x 15 inch) jelly roll pan with parchment.
Sift the flour, baking powder and salt. Whisk the yolks with 50 g sugar until pale, then whisk in the oil, milk and ube flavoring, then the flour mixture.
Beat the egg whites with the cream of tartar until foamy, add 70 g sugar gradually and beat to stiff, glossy peaks. Fold into the batter gently in three additions.
Spread evenly in the pan and bake until the top springs back when touched.
Loosen the edges, turn the cake out onto a clean sheet of parchment, peel off the baking paper and roll it up from the short end with the new paper while warm. Cool rolled.
Mix the ube halaya with the butter until spreadable. Unroll the cake, spread the filling evenly, leaving a 2 cm (1 inch) border at the far end, and roll it up again firmly.
Wrap in the parchment and chill, seam side down, until set.
Dust with powdered sugar, trim the ends and slice.

tips: Rolling the sponge while it is warm trains it into shape so it does not crack later. Keep the roll in the fridge for up to 3 days.

title: Pianono
intro: A light sponge cake rolled up with a simple filling of butter and sugar, with more sugar sprinkled over the top. Soft, sweet and buttery, it is a classic bakery merienda.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 180°C (350°F). Line a 25 x 38 cm (10 x 15 inch) jelly roll pan with parchment.
Sift the flour, baking powder and salt. Beat the yolks with 60 g sugar until thick and pale, then beat in the milk, melted butter and vanilla. Fold in the flour.
Beat the egg whites until foamy, add the remaining 60 g sugar gradually and beat to stiff, glossy peaks. Fold into the yolk mixture gently in three additions.
Spread evenly in the pan and bake until golden and springy.
Turn the cake out onto parchment sprinkled with sugar, peel off the baking paper, and roll up from the short end with the new paper while warm. Cool rolled.
Unroll, spread with softened butter, sprinkle with sugar and roll up again snugly.
Brush the outside with a little more butter if you like, sprinkle with sugar and slice.

tips: Pianono is best eaten the day it is made. Wrap leftovers tightly and keep at room temperature for a day, or chill for up to 3 days.

title: Brazo de mercedes
intro: A soft, golden meringue sheet rolled around a rich custard filling made from the egg yolks and condensed milk. Sweet, airy and creamy, it is served chilled.

steps.text: Make the filling: whisk the yolks and condensed milk in a nonstick pan, add the butter and cook over low heat, stirring constantly, until thick and spreadable, about 12 minutes. Stir in the vanilla and cool.
Heat the oven to 175°C (350°F). Line a 25 x 38 cm (10 x 15 inch) jelly roll pan with parchment and grease the paper well.
Beat the egg whites with the cream of tartar until foamy. Add the sugar a spoonful at a time and beat to stiff, glossy peaks. Beat in the vanilla.
Spread the meringue evenly in the pan and bake until golden brown on top.
Cool in the pan for 10 minutes. Dust a sheet of parchment with powdered sugar and turn the meringue out onto it, browned side down. Peel off the baking paper.
Spread the filling over the meringue, leaving a 2 cm (1 inch) border along one long edge. Using the paper to help, roll up toward the bare edge.
Wrap in the paper and chill until set.
Dust with more powdered sugar and slice with a knife dipped in hot water.

tips: Do not worry if the meringue cracks a little as you roll; the powdered sugar hides it. Keep in the fridge and eat within 3 days.

title: Yema cake
intro: Soft chiffon layers covered in a thick, glossy yema frosting of condensed milk and egg yolks, then topped with grated cheese. Sweet, creamy and salty all at once.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 160°C (325°F). Line the bottoms of two 20 cm (8 inch) round pans with parchment; do not grease the sides.
Sift the flour, baking powder and salt. Whisk the yolks with 60 g sugar until pale, then whisk in the oil, evaporated milk and vanilla, and the flour mixture.
Beat the egg whites with the cream of tartar until foamy, add 100 g sugar gradually and beat to stiff, glossy peaks. Fold into the batter in three additions.
Divide between the pans and bake until springy and a skewer comes out clean.
Invert the pans and cool completely, then release the layers.

For the frosting, whisk the condensed milk, yolks and evaporated milk in a nonstick pan, add the butter and cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, until thick enough to hold soft ridges, about 15 minutes. Stir in the vanilla and cool until just warm and spreadable.
Spread frosting over one layer, top with the second, then cover the top and sides with the rest.
Sprinkle the grated cheese over the top. Chill to set before slicing.

tips: The frosting thickens as it cools; if it gets too stiff to spread, warm it gently with a splash of evaporated milk. Keep the cake in the fridge for up to 4 days.

title: Mango cake
intro: Light chiffon layers filled and covered with whipped cream and plenty of sweet, ripe mango. Cool, fruity and not heavy, it is a favorite for birthdays in mango season.

items.name: large ripe mangoes
items.note: about 1 kg, carabao mangoes if you can find them

steps.text: Heat the oven to 160°C (325°F). Line the bottoms of two 20 cm (8 inch) round pans with parchment; do not grease the sides.
Sift the flour, baking powder and salt. Whisk the yolks with 60 g sugar until pale, whisk in the oil, milk and vanilla, then the flour mixture.
Beat the egg whites with the cream of tartar until foamy, add 90 g sugar gradually and beat to stiff, glossy peaks. Fold into the batter in three additions.
Divide between the pans and bake until springy and a skewer comes out clean.
Invert the pans and cool completely, then release the layers.
Slice the cheeks off the mangoes. Dice one mango for the filling and cut the rest into thin slices for the top.
Whip the cream with the powdered sugar and vanilla to firm peaks.

Set one layer on a plate, spread with a layer of cream and scatter the diced mango over. Top with the second layer and cover the top and sides with the remaining cream. Arrange the mango slices over the top.
Chill until the cream is set and the cake is cold.

tips: Use mangoes that are ripe but still firm so the slices hold their shape. The cake is best within 2 days; keep it covered in the fridge.
